points.formula: I am · He/She/It is · You/We/They are

examples.en: I am a student.
My parents are at home.
Is she your sister?

mistakes.why: She is singular, so the verb is is, not are.
An adjective like happy cannot follow the subject directly. English needs the verb to be: I am happy.

points.title: The verb to be (am / is / are)
points.when: To say who or what someone is, and to describe jobs, places, ages and feelings.
points.body: Use am with I, is with he, she, it and singular nouns, and are with you, we, they and plural nouns. For the negative, add not (isn't, aren't). For a question, put the verb before the subject: Are you ready? Before an adjective, English always needs the verb to be: She is tired.

points.formula: S + V(s/es) · S + do/does + not + V · Do/Does + S + V?

examples.en: She works in a bank.
I don't drink coffee.
Does he play football?

mistakes.why: The subject he is third person singular, so the verb needs -s: works.
After doesn't, use the base verb. The -s is already in does, so like takes no -s.

points.title: Present simple
points.when: For habits, repeated actions, facts that are always true, and fixed timetables.
points.body: With he, she, it or a singular noun, add -s or -es to the verb (works, watches, goes). For negatives and questions, use do or does + the base verb: She doesn't work. Does she work? When does is already there, the main verb takes no -s.

points.formula: a + consonant sound · an + vowel sound · the + specific or known noun

examples.en: I saw a cat. The cat was black.
She is an engineer.
The sun rises in the east.

mistakes.why: The h in honest is silent, so the word starts with a vowel sound and needs an.

mistakes.right: I want to be an engineer.
mistakes.why: A job after be needs a or an when it refers to one person: an engineer.

points.title: Articles: a / an / the
points.when: Use a or an when you mention one thing for the first time or mean any one of many. Use the when the listener knows which one you mean, when you have mentioned it before, or when there is only one.
points.body: A and an go only with singular countable nouns. Choose by the first sound, not the first letter: an hour (the h is silent), a university (it starts with a /j/ sound). Use the for something both speakers can identify, or for something unique: the sun, the moon. Plural and uncountable nouns used in a general sense take no article: Cats like milk.

points.formula: N + s / es / ies · irregular: man → men, child → children

examples.en: There are three boxes on the floor.
Many children like cartoons.
We visited two cities.

mistakes.why: Child has an irregular plural: children.
Information is uncountable, so it takes no -s, and it goes with much, not many.

points.title: Plural nouns
points.when: When you talk about two or more people or things.
points.body: Most nouns add -s. Nouns ending in -s, -sh, -ch, -x and many ending in -o add -es (buses, watches, boxes, tomatoes). A consonant + y changes to -ies (city → cities). Some plurals are irregular and must be learned: man → men, woman → women, child → children, foot → feet, tooth → teeth, person → people, mouse → mice. Uncountable nouns such as information, advice and furniture have no plural.

points.formula: at + clock time or exact place · on + day or surface · in + month, year, season, or inside space

examples.en: The meeting is at 9 a.m. on Monday.
I was born in 2005.
Your phone is on the desk.

mistakes.why: Days of the week take on.
Parts of the day take in: in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening. The exception is at night.

points.title: Prepositions of time and place: in / on / at
points.when: To say when something happens or where something is.
points.body: Time: at + a clock time or a point (at 7 o'clock, at night, at the weekend in British English); on + a day or date (on Monday, on 5 May); in + a month, year, season or part of the day (in May, in 2025, in summer, in the morning). Place: at + a point (at the bus stop); on + a surface (on the table); in + inside a space or area (in the box, in the city).

points.formula: There is + singular or uncountable N · There are + plural N

examples.en: There is a bank near my house.
There are 30 students in my class.
Is there any milk in the fridge?

mistakes.wrong: It has a park near here.
mistakes.right: There is a park near here.
mistakes.why: To say that something exists in a place, use there is. It has means that a thing owns something.
People is plural, so the verb is are.

points.title: There is / There are
points.when: To say that something exists or is in a place.
points.body: Use there is or there are, not have or it has, to say that something exists somewhere. The verb agrees with the noun that comes after it: There is a book. There are two books. In a list, it agrees with the first noun: There is a pen and two books. Questions: Is there…? Are there…?

points.formula: S + can/could + base verb

examples.en: She can speak three languages.
I couldn't sleep last night.
Could you open the window, please?

mistakes.why: After can, use the base verb without -s: swim.
Can is followed directly by the base verb, without to.

points.title: Can / Could
points.when: To talk about ability, to ask for or give permission, and to make polite requests.
points.body: Can is for ability now (I can swim) and permission (You can sit here). Could is for ability in the past (I could read at four) and for more polite requests (Could you help me?). After can and could, always use the base verb: no to and no -s. Can and could never change for he, she or it.

points.formula: S + V + O + Place + Time · Adjectives come before nouns

examples.en: I bought a new phone yesterday.
She always drinks coffee in the morning.
He is always late.

mistakes.why: In English, the adjective comes before the noun: a red car.
A frequency adverb goes before the main verb, not after it.

points.title: Basic word order
points.when: Whenever you build a sentence, so that it sounds natural in English.
points.body: The basic order is Subject + Verb + Object + Place + Time: I met Tom at the station yesterday. Adjectives come before the noun they describe: a red car. Frequency adverbs (always, often, never) go before the main verb but after the verb to be: She always walks. She is always late.

points.formula: S + V2/V-ed · S + didn't + V · Did + S + V?

examples.en: I visited the old city last summer.
She didn't come to class yesterday.
Did you see the match?

mistakes.why: Did already shows the past, so the main verb stays in the base form: go.
Yesterday is a finished past time, so the verb must be in the past simple: went.

points.title: Past simple
points.when: For actions that started and finished at a definite time in the past.
points.body: Regular verbs add -ed (worked, studied, stopped). Irregular verbs have their own forms and must be learned (go → went, buy → bought, see → saw). For negatives and questions, use did + the base verb: I didn't go. Did you see it? The verb to be has two past forms: was (I, he, she, it) and were (you, we, they).

points.formula: S + am/is/are + V-ing

examples.en: I'm studying English now.
Look! It's raining.
We're meeting the client tomorrow.

mistakes.why: The continuous needs the -ing form after is: cooking.
Know describes a state, not an action, so it stays in the simple form.

points.title: Present continuous
points.when: For actions happening now or around now, temporary situations, and future plans that are already arranged.
points.body: Form it with am, is or are + verb-ing. Common signals are now, right now, at the moment, Look! and Listen! Stative verbs, which describe states rather than actions (know, like, want, need, believe, understand), are not normally used in the continuous: I know, not I'm knowing.

points.formula: adj-er than · more + adj + than · the adj-est · the most + adj

examples.en: This phone is cheaper than that one.
She is the best student in the class.
My town is as quiet as a village.

mistakes.why: Cheaper is already comparative, so do not add more.
Good has irregular forms: better and the best.

points.title: Comparatives and superlatives
points.when: To compare two or more people or things.
points.body: Short adjectives (one syllable, or two syllables ending in -y) add -er and -est: cheap → cheaper → the cheapest; happy → happier → the happiest. Longer adjectives use more and most: more expensive, the most expensive. Some forms are irregular: good → better → the best; bad → worse → the worst; far → farther/further → the farthest/furthest. To say two things are equal, use as + adjective + as.

points.formula: many/few + countable N · much/little + uncountable N · some/any/a lot of: both

examples.en: How much money do you need?
I have a few friends in Canada.
Would you like some tea?

mistakes.why: Money is uncountable, so use much, not many.
Luggage is uncountable, so it has no plural form.

points.title: Countable and uncountable nouns; quantifiers
points.when: To talk about amounts: how much or how many.
points.body: With countable nouns use many, a few, few and a number of. With uncountable nouns (water, money, information, advice, furniture, luggage) use much, a little, little and an amount of. A lot of, lots of, some and any work with both. Some is usual in positive sentences and offers; any is usual in negatives and questions. A few and a little mean 'some, enough'; few and little mean 'not enough'.

points.formula: S + will + V · S + am/is/are going to + V

examples.en: I'm hungry. — I'll make you a sandwich.
We're going to visit Japan next month.
Look at the sky! It's going to rain.

mistakes.why: After will, use the base verb without to.

mistakes.wrong: She going to buy a car.
mistakes.right: She is going to buy a car.
mistakes.why: Going to needs the verb to be before it: she is going to.

points.title: Will and be going to
points.when: To talk about the future: decisions made now, predictions, and plans.
points.body: Use will for decisions made at the moment of speaking (I'll get it!), promises, offers, and general predictions (I think it will rain). Use be going to for plans you made before (I'm going to study abroad) and for predictions based on what you can see now (Look at those clouds. It's going to rain).

points.formula: S + must/should + V · S + have/has to + V

examples.en: You should drink more water.
You mustn't smoke here.
You don't have to come if you're busy.

mistakes.wrong: You must to wear a helmet.
mistakes.why: Must is followed directly by the base verb, without to.

mistakes.wrong: She have to work on Saturday.
mistakes.right: She has to work on Saturday.
mistakes.why: With she, have to becomes has to.

points.title: Must / Should / Have to
points.when: To talk about obligation, advice and things that are not allowed.
points.body: Should gives advice. Must shows a strong obligation, often from the speaker or from rules. Have to shows an obligation that comes from outside, such as a job or a law. Be careful with the negatives: mustn't means it is not allowed, but don't have to means it is not necessary. After must and should, use the base verb.

points.formula: I/me/my/mine · he/him/his/his · she/her/her/hers · they/them/their/theirs

examples.en: This is my bag. That one is yours.
Can you help me?
She made the cake herself.

mistakes.why: The subject of a sentence needs subject pronouns: he and I. It is also polite to put I last.
With no noun after it, you need the possessive pronoun mine, not my.

points.title: Pronouns and possessives
points.when: To replace a noun, or to show who something belongs to.
points.body: Subject pronouns (I, he, she, we, they) come before the verb. Object pronouns (me, him, her, us, them) come after a verb or preposition. Possessive adjectives (my, his, her, our, their) come before a noun. Possessive pronouns (mine, his, hers, ours, theirs) stand alone and replace possessive + noun. Reflexive pronouns (myself, himself…) are used when the subject and object are the same person.

points.formula: S + have/has + V3/V-ed

examples.en: I have already finished my homework.
She has worked here since 2019.
Have you ever been to Korea?

mistakes.why: Yesterday is a finished time, so use the past simple: I saw him yesterday.
After has, use the past participle: gone, not went.

points.title: Present perfect (vs. past simple)
points.when: For experiences, actions that have just finished, situations that started in the past and continue now, and past actions with a result now.
points.body: Form it with have or has + the past participle. Do not use it with a finished past time such as yesterday, last year or in 2020; use the past simple instead. Common signals are just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, so far, recently and up to now.

points.formula: S + be + V3 (+ by O)

examples.en: This bridge was built in 1900.
English is spoken all over the world.
The meeting will be held on Monday.

mistakes.wrong: The letter was wrote by Nam.
mistakes.right: The letter was written by Nam.
mistakes.why: The passive uses the past participle: written, not wrote.

mistakes.right: The report must be sent today.
mistakes.why: A report cannot send itself, so the verb must be passive: must be sent.

points.title: The passive voice
points.when: When the person or thing receiving the action matters more, or when we do not know or do not need to say who did it.
points.body: Form it with the verb to be in the right tense + the past participle: is made, was built, has been sent, will be held, must be signed. Add by + the doer only if it is useful. A tip for exam questions: if the subject is a thing that receives the action and there is no object after the gap, the answer is usually passive.

points.formula: 0: If + present, present · 1: If + present, will + V · 2: If + past, would + V

examples.en: If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel the trip.
If I were you, I would apply for that job.
examples.hl: If I were you ... would apply

examples.en: If you heat water to 100°C, it boils.

mistakes.wrong: If it will rain, I will stay home.
mistakes.right: If it rains, I will stay home.
mistakes.why: In a first conditional, the if-clause uses the present simple, not will.

mistakes.wrong: If I am rich, I would buy a big house.
mistakes.right: If I were rich, I would buy a big house.
mistakes.why: An imagined present situation needs the second conditional: If + past (were), would + verb.

points.title: Conditionals: zero, first, second
points.when: Zero: facts that are always true. First: real possibilities in the future. Second: imagined situations in the present.
points.body: Zero conditional: If + present, present (If you heat ice, it melts). First conditional: If + present, will + base verb (If it rains, I will stay home); do not use will in the if-clause. Second conditional: If + past, would + base verb (If I had money, I would travel); with be, use were for every subject (If I were you…). Unless means if … not.

points.formula: N (person) + who · N (thing) + which · that: both · whose + N · where: place

examples.en: The woman who lives next door is a doctor.
This is the phone which I bought yesterday.
That's the man whose car was stolen.

mistakes.why: The man is a person, so use who, not which.

mistakes.wrong: The river, that runs through the city, is very long.
mistakes.right: The river, which runs through the city, is very long.
mistakes.why: After a comma (a non-defining clause), use which, not that.

points.title: Relative clauses (who / which / that / whose / where)
points.when: To add information about the noun that comes just before.
points.body: Use who for people, which for things, and that for both in defining clauses. Whose + noun shows possession. Where means 'in or at which' for places. In a non-defining clause, which is set off by commas, you cannot use that. You can leave out the relative pronoun when it is the object of the clause: the phone (that) I bought.

points.formula: enjoy/avoid/finish/mind/suggest + V-ing · want/decide/plan/hope/agree + to V

examples.en: I enjoy reading in the evening.
She decided to study abroad.
We look forward to meeting you.

mistakes.wrong: I look forward to hear from you.
mistakes.right: I look forward to hearing from you.
mistakes.why: In look forward to, to is a preposition, so it is followed by -ing.
Avoid is followed by -ing, not by to + verb.

points.title: Gerund or infinitive
points.when: To choose the correct form of a verb that follows another verb or a preposition.
points.body: After a preposition, always use -ing (interested in learning, before leaving, look forward to meeting). Some verbs take -ing: enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, suggest, consider, keep, practise, recommend. Others take to + verb: want, decide, plan, hope, agree, refuse, promise, afford, manage, need, would like. A few change meaning: stop doing (quit) and stop to do (pause in order to do); remember doing (a memory of the past) and remember to do (not forget a task).

points.formula: Conjunction + CLAUSE (S + V) · Preposition + NOUN / V-ing

examples.en: Although it was late, she kept working.
Despite the rain, the match continued.
The flight was canceled due to bad weather.

mistakes.wrong: Despite it rained, we went out.
mistakes.right: Although it rained, we went out.
mistakes.why: It rained is a clause, so you need the conjunction although.
The traffic is a noun phrase, so you need the preposition because of.

points.title: Conjunction or preposition (although / despite …)
points.when: To choose between a conjunction and a preposition that have the same meaning. Look at what follows: a clause or a noun phrase.
points.body: Pairs with the same meaning: although/though/even though (conjunctions) and despite/in spite of (prepositions); because/since/as (conjunctions) and because of/due to/owing to (prepositions); while (conjunction) and during (preposition). A conjunction is followed by a clause with a subject and verb. A preposition is followed by a noun, a noun phrase or -ing.

points.formula: Singular subject → V(s/es) · plural subject → base verb

examples.en: The list of candidates is on the desk.
Every student has a laptop.
A number of employees are working from home.

mistakes.wrong: The quality of these products are high.
mistakes.right: The quality of these products is high.
mistakes.why: The real subject is the quality, which is singular, so use is.
Everyone takes a singular verb: has.

points.title: Subject–verb agreement
points.when: To make the verb agree with the real subject of the sentence.
points.body: Find the real subject. A prepositional phrase between the subject and the verb does not change it: The list of names is… Each, every, everyone and nobody take a singular verb. Uncountable nouns take a singular verb. A number of + plural noun takes a plural verb, but the number of takes a singular verb. With either…or and neither…nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject.

points.formula: N: -tion, -ment, -ness, -ity · V: -ize, -en, -ify · Adj: -ful, -ous, -ive, -able · Adv: adj + -ly

examples.en: We made a final decision.
The new system works efficiently.
The room is available now.

mistakes.why: The word describes how she speaks, so you need the adverb fluently.
Before the noun plan, you need an adjective: successful.

points.title: Word forms (noun / verb / adjective / adverb)
points.when: To choose the right part of speech for a gap, based on its position in the sentence.
points.body: After an article or a possessive, use a noun (the decision). Before a noun, use an adjective (a successful plan). After be, become or seem, use an adjective (is available). To describe a verb, an adjective or a whole sentence, use an adverb (work efficiently, highly qualified). Between have or be and a past participle, use an adverb (has recently opened). Common endings help: nouns -tion, -ment, -ness, -ity; verbs -ize, -en, -ify; adjectives -ful, -ous, -ive, -able; adverbs -ly.

points.formula: S + had + V3

examples.en: When we arrived, the film had already started.
She had worked there for ten years before she retired.
By the time I called, he had left.

mistakes.wrong: When I arrived, the train already left.
mistakes.right: When I arrived, the train had already left.
mistakes.why: The train left before I arrived, so the earlier action needs had left.
After had, use the past participle: seen, not saw.

points.title: Past perfect
points.when: For an action that happened before another action or time in the past.
points.body: When you talk about two past events, use had + past participle for the earlier one and the past simple for the later one. It often appears with before, after, by the time, when and already. Pattern: By the time + past simple, subject + had + past participle.

points.formula: If + had + V3, would have + V3 · mixed: If + had + V3, would + V (now)

examples.en: If I had left earlier, I wouldn't have missed the bus.
If she had studied medicine, she would be a doctor now.
Had I known, I would have helped.

mistakes.wrong: If I would have known, I would have come.
mistakes.right: If I had known, I would have come.
mistakes.why: The if-clause does not take would. Use had + past participle.

mistakes.wrong: If he had asked me, I would help him.
mistakes.right: If he had asked me, I would have helped him.
mistakes.why: The result is in the past, so use would have + past participle.

points.title: Third and mixed conditionals
points.when: To imagine a different past (often for regret), or a past condition with a result now.
points.body: Third conditional: If + had + past participle, would have + past participle, for something that did not happen in the past (If I had studied, I would have passed). Mixed conditional: a past condition with a present result (If I had taken that job, I would be rich now). In formal English, Had I known means If I had known.

points.formula: said (that) + lùi thì · asked if/whether · told sb to V

examples.en: He said that he was tired.
She asked me where I lived.
The teacher told us to be quiet.

mistakes.wrong: She asked where did I live.
mistakes.why: A reported question uses statement word order: where I lived, without did.

mistakes.right: He told me that... / He said that...
mistakes.why: Say is not followed directly by a person. Use told me, or said that.

points.title: Reported speech
points.when: To tell someone what another person said or asked.
points.body: When the reporting verb is in the past (said, told, asked), move the tense back one step: am/is → was, will → would, can → could, present simple → past simple, past simple → past perfect. Change pronouns and time and place words as needed: now → then, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, here → there. Reported questions use statement word order: She asked where I lived.

points.formula: V-ing (active) · V3 (passive) · Having + V3 (earlier action)

examples.en: The woman sitting next to me is a lawyer.
Products made in the country are popular.
Having finished her work, she went home.

mistakes.wrong: The report writing by Mr. Kim...
mistakes.right: The report written by Mr. Kim...
mistakes.why: The report was written by someone, so the meaning is passive: written.

mistakes.right: While I was walking home, the rain started.
mistakes.why: Walking home has no subject of its own, so it describes the main subject, the rain. The rain was not walking, so you need a full clause.

points.title: Participle clauses
points.when: To make relative or adverb clauses shorter.
points.body: Shortened relative clauses: active meaning → -ing (the man sitting there = who is sitting there); passive meaning → past participle (products made in Japan = which are made in Japan). Shortened adverb clauses work only when both clauses have the same subject: Walking home, I met an old friend. Having + past participle shows that one action happened first: Having finished the work, she went home.

points.formula: wish + past (present) · wish + had V3 (past) · wish + would (want change)

examples.en: I wish I spoke English fluently.
She wishes she hadn't said that.
If only it would stop raining!

mistakes.why: A wish about the present moves the verb back to the past: were.

mistakes.wrong: I wish I didn't eat so much last night.
mistakes.right: I wish I hadn't eaten so much last night.
mistakes.why: A wish about the past needs had + past participle: hadn't eaten.

points.title: Wish / If only
points.when: To say that you want reality to be different.
points.body: For the present, use wish + past (I wish I had more time, but I don't). With be, use were: I wish I were taller. For the past, use wish + had + past participle: I wish I had studied harder. To complain that someone or something will not change, use wish + would: I wish it would stop raining. If only has the same meaning but is stronger.

points.formula: So/Neither + auxiliary + S · Not only + auxiliary + S + V, but also...

examples.en: I love durian. — So do I.
She didn't come. — Neither did he.
Never have I seen such a beautiful sunset.

mistakes.why: After So, the auxiliary comes before the subject: So am I.
When Never starts the sentence, put the auxiliary before the subject: have I.

points.title: Basic inversion (So / Neither, Not only …)
points.when: To say 'me too' or 'me neither', and to add emphasis in formal writing.
points.body: To agree with a positive sentence: So + auxiliary + subject (I like tea. So do I). To agree with a negative sentence: Neither/Nor + auxiliary + subject (I can't swim. Neither can I). When a sentence starts with a negative word such as Never, Rarely, Seldom, Not only or Only then, put the auxiliary before the subject.

points.formula: should/could/might/must/can't + have + V3

examples.en: You should have told me earlier.
He must have forgotten the meeting.
She can't have finished already.

mistakes.why: To talk about the past, a modal needs have + past participle: should have told.
After must, use the base form have, never has.

points.title: Modal perfects (should have, must have …)
points.when: To talk about regrets and to make guesses about the past.
points.body: Should have + past participle: it was a good idea, but it did not happen. Shouldn't have + past participle: it happened, but it was a bad idea. Must have + past participle: you are almost sure it happened. Can't/couldn't have + past participle: you are sure it did not happen. Might/may/could have + past participle: it possibly happened.

points.formula: however · therefore · moreover · otherwise · as a result · in addition · for example

examples.en: The hotel was expensive. However, the service was excellent.
It rained heavily. As a result, the match was canceled.
Please reply by Friday. Otherwise, we will give the seat to someone else.

mistakes.wrong: The plan is good, however it is expensive.
mistakes.right: The plan is good. However, it is expensive.
mistakes.why: However cannot join two clauses with a comma. Start a new sentence, or use a semicolon.

mistakes.wrong: He was sick. Therefore he came to work.
mistakes.right: He was sick. However, he came to work.
mistakes.why: Coming to work while sick is a contrast, not a result, so the linker is however.

points.title: Linking words and discourse markers
points.when: To connect ideas across sentences in a paragraph.
points.body: Contrast: however, nevertheless, on the other hand. Result: therefore, as a result, consequently. Addition: moreover, furthermore, in addition. Condition: otherwise (if not). Example: for example, for instance. These words usually start a new sentence and are followed by a comma. They link two sentences; unlike conjunctions such as but or so, they cannot join two clauses with only a comma.

points.formula: det + adv + adj + N + N (+ prep phrase)

examples.en: our highly experienced sales team
a two-week training program
the company's annual performance review

mistakes.why: A compound adjective with a number stays singular: two-week.
A noun that describes another noun is usually singular: customer service.

points.title: Complex noun phrases
points.when: To read and build the long noun phrases found in work and academic texts.
points.body: Order: determiner (the, our) + adverb (highly) + adjective (experienced) + noun modifier (sales) + head noun (team). A noun used before another noun works like an adjective and is usually singular: a customer service desk. Compound adjectives with numbers are joined by a hyphen and stay singular: a ten-minute break.

points.formula: suggest / recommend / insist / require / It is essential that + S + base verb

examples.en: The doctor recommended that he rest for a week.
It is essential that every employee attend the meeting.
She insisted that we be on time.

mistakes.wrong: I suggest that he goes home.
mistakes.right: I suggest that he go home.
mistakes.why: After suggest that, use the base verb for every subject: go.

mistakes.wrong: It is important that she is here.
mistakes.right: It is important that she be here.
mistakes.why: After It is important that, use be for every subject.

points.title: The subjunctive (suggest that + base verb)
points.when: In formal English, after verbs and phrases of suggestion, demand and necessity.
points.body: After suggest, recommend, insist, demand, request, require and It is important/essential/necessary that…, the verb in the that-clause is the base form for every subject: no -s and no tense change. The negative is not + base verb (that he not be late). British English often uses should + verb instead.

points.formula: It is/was + X + that/who... · What + S + V + is/was + X

examples.en: It was my mother who taught me to cook.
What I love about the capital city is the food.
It is in the morning that I study best.
examples.hl: It is in the morning that

mistakes.wrong: It was him that he called me.
mistakes.right: It was he who called me. / It was him who called me.
mistakes.why: Do not repeat the subject after who or that.

mistakes.wrong: What I need it is sleep.
mistakes.why: The what-clause is already the subject, so do not add it.

points.title: Cleft sentences (It is … that / What … is)
points.when: To give special emphasis to one part of a sentence.
points.body: It-cleft: It is/was + the part you want to emphasise + that/who + the rest: It was Alex who won the prize. What-cleft: What + subject + verb + is/was + the emphasised part: What I need is a holiday.

points.formula: No sooner had S V3 than... · Hardly had S V3 when... · Only after/when... + inversion · Should + S + V (= If)

examples.en: No sooner had I arrived than it started to rain.
examples.hl: No sooner had I arrived than

examples.en: Only after the meeting did I understand the plan.
Should you have any questions, please contact us.

mistakes.wrong: No sooner I had arrived than...
mistakes.right: No sooner had I arrived than...
mistakes.why: After No sooner, put had before the subject.
Hardly goes with when, not than.

points.title: Advanced inversion (No sooner, Hardly …)
points.when: In formal writing and harder exam questions.
points.body: No sooner had + subject + past participle + than + past simple: one thing happened just after another. Hardly/Scarcely had + subject + past participle + when + past simple. Only after/when/if + clause or phrase, then invert the main clause. Under no circumstances + inversion means 'never'. Should + subject + verb means If + subject + should + verb, a formal first conditional common in business emails.

points.formula: I think so / I hope not · one/ones · do so · auxiliary replaces a whole phrase

examples.en: Will it rain tomorrow? — I hope not.
I don't like this shirt. Can I see the blue one?
She said she would call, and she did.

mistakes.why: After think, use so to replace the clause, not yes.
With hope, the negative is I hope not.

points.title: Ellipsis and substitution
points.when: To avoid repeating words and to sound natural.
points.body: So and not replace a whole clause after think, hope, expect, guess and be afraid: I think so. I hope not. One and ones replace a countable noun already mentioned: I like the red one. Do so replaces a verb phrase in formal English. An auxiliary can stand for a whole verb phrase: She can swim, but I can't.

points.formula: may/might/could · seem/appear · tend to · likely · It is possible that

examples.en: The results seem to suggest a link.
Prices are likely to rise next year.
I was wondering if you could help me.

mistakes.why: Be likely is followed by to + verb.

mistakes.right: Students tend to study at night.
mistakes.why: Tend is followed by to + verb.

points.title: Hedging and softening
points.when: To show how certain you are, in academic writing and in polite conversation.
points.body: Fluent speakers rarely state things as absolutely certain. Use may, might or could (possibly), seem/appear to, tend to, be likely/unlikely to and It is possible that… to make claims softer and more accurate. For polite requests, I was wondering if you could… is softer than Can you…?

points.formula: formal: request, assist, purchase, inform · informal: ask, help, buy, tell

examples.en: Please do not hesitate to contact us.
We regret to inform you that the position has been filled.
Hey, can you send me that file?

mistakes.wrong: Hi boss, gimme the report pls.
mistakes.right: Dear Mr. Lee, could you please send me the report?
mistakes.why: A message to a manager needs a polite, complete, formal sentence.

mistakes.wrong: We are sorry to tell you...
mistakes.why: Formal letters use the fixed phrase We regret to inform you.

points.title: Formal and informal register
points.when: To choose words that fit the situation: a work email, a job application or a message to a friend.
points.body: Formal English uses longer, often Latin-based words (purchase for buy, assist for help, require for need, inform for tell), avoids contractions (I am, not I'm), and uses complete sentences and the passive. Informal English uses phrasal verbs (find out, get), contractions and short sentences. A work email starts with Dear Mr./Ms. + family name and ends with Best regards or Sincerely.
